MMDA CHIEF’S BLAME GAME MISSES THE POINT

MMDA Acting Chair Romando Artes’ recent statement blaming the Dolomite Beach for flooding along Taft Avenue is not only technically questionable—it reeks of political deflection.

Let’s set the record straight.

1. The Dolomite Beach is part of a Supreme Court-mandated cleanup.

The Manila Bay Rehabilitation Program stems from a 2008 Mandamus by the Supreme Court ordering 13 agencies—including the MMDA—to clean up and rehabilitate Manila Bay until its waters are safe for swimming. The Dolomite Beach, while controversial to some, was a visible and symbolic part of this larger compliance effort—one that millions of Metro residents and tourists have come to enjoy.

2. Why blame success?

Instead of seeing the dolomite development as a burden, why not see it for what it is—one of the few successful and visible outcomes of a long-overdue government effort? It attracted local and international attention, raised public awareness, and boosted the morale of environmental campaigns.

3. If the sewerage system is failing, fix it.

If indeed the diversion of water flow toward treatment canals is causing flooding, then that’s a failure of engineering planning, not of beachfront beautification. Why hasn’t MMDA improved the capacity of the canal system instead of scapegoating a feature project? Artes, as MMDA chair, had ample time and authority to resolve drainage limitations. Blaming a beach for blocked outflows is like blaming curtains for a leaky roof.

4. Stop politicizing a Supreme Court order.

Let’s not forget—it was the Duterte administration that had the political will to operationalize the Court’s ruling. The same administration boldly shut down Boracay to fix its environmental mess, despite backlash. Say what you will about its shortcomings, but it did act where previous governments hesitated.

So, the real question is: Is MMDA’s sudden critique of the dolomite beach technical, or political?

Because from where we stand, blaming Duterte-era projects for current problems is becoming a lazy narrative—a convenient distraction from present-day inaction.

If the current administration is truly committed to environmental rehabilitation, it should build on what has been started—not demolish it with talking points.
_Butch Ruiz Baliao

Four signs na kinakabahan na ang mga dolomite-natics:

1. Kapag ayaw mo ng dolomite beach, gusto mo ng basura sa Manila Bay. 

May dolomite beach o wala, magkakabasura at dumi sa Manila Bay kung kulang ang sewage treatment plants at iba pang engineering at environmental solutions para salain ang basura: mga dagdag na proyekto na pwede sanang pinondohan ng P389-M pesos na sinayang sa dolomite beach.

2. Hindi dolomite beach ang dahilan ng baha sa Maynila, kundi yung pagsasara ng tatlong malalaking lagusan ng tubig.

Kaya tinakpan yung tatlong malaking lagusan ng tubig dahil mismo sa kabuuang plano ng dolomite beach at karatig na lugar sa Manila Bay. Imbes na tinakpan yung tatlong lagusan ng tubig, sana ginamit nalang yung P389-M pondo ng dolomite beach para sa dagdag sewage treatment plants sa mga malalaking lagusang ito para mas mabilis dumaloy, malinis ang tubig palabas ng Manila Bay at hindi magbaha sa mga kalapit na lugar sa Maynila.

3. Kasama ang dolomite beach sa SC continuing mandamus para linisin ang Manila Bay kaya tama lang na pondohan yan. 

Hindi kasama ang dolomite beach sa continuing mandamus ng SC para linisin ang Manila Bay. Wala nga ito sa NEDA Manila Bay rehabilitation master plan, at walang ambag ito sa layunin ng mandamus na linisin ang kalidad ng tubig na dumadaloy sa Manila Bay. Hindi rin kasama sa mandamus ang improvement ng mental health ng mga Pilipino.

4. Dapat imbestigahan din ang mga reklamasyon sa Manila Bay at flood control projects sa buong Pilipinas imbes na yang dolomite beach na yan. 

Tama naman. Darating din tayo diyan. Abangan.
